content_blocks.title: Why Resource Limits Matter
content_blocks.content: Think of resource limits as seatbelts for your Linux system. You don't put them on because you expect a crash — you put them on because a single失控 process can take down everything. As a blue teamer, mastering ulimit isn't optional; it's how you turn a potential DoS into a contained incident.

content_blocks.title: Understanding Linux Resource Limits
content_blocks.content: Linux enforces resource limits through the RLIMIT mechanism — kernel-enforced ceilings on what a process or user can consume. Two types exist: **soft limits** (the current enforced value, user-raisable up to the hard limit) and **hard limits** (the ceiling, root-only to increase). These cover CPU time, memory, open files, processes, and more. The `ulimit` shell builtin queries and sets these for the current session, while `/etc/security/limits.conf` provides persistent, PAM-enforced defaults.

content_blocks.title: Teach Me Like I'm 10: Resource Limits
content_blocks.content: Imagine a buffet where each person can take only 2 plates (soft limit) but the manager can allow up to 5 plates (hard limit). If someone tries to grab 6 plates, they're stopped. That's ulimit — it stops greedy programs from eating all the computer's food (memory, files, CPU) so everyone else can still eat.

content_blocks.title: Checking and Setting ulimit Values
content_blocks.content:
```bash
# View all current soft limits
ulimit -a

# View specific limits
ulimit -n    # max open files
ulimit -u    # max user processes
ulimit -v    # max virtual memory (KB)

# Set soft limit for open files (current session only)
ulimit -Sn 4096

# Set hard limit (requires root or previous higher hard limit)
ulimit -Hn 8192

# View limits for a running process
prlimit -n -p $(pgrep nginx | head -1)
```

content_blocks.title: Real-World: Preventing Fork Bomb DoS
content_blocks.content: A fork bomb (`:(){ :|:& };:`) can spawn thousands of processes in seconds, exhausting PID space and memory. By setting `nproc` (max processes per user) in limits.conf, you contain the blast radius. A web server user with `nproc 512` can fork at most 512 processes — the bomb hits the ceiling and the kernel kills excess processes, leaving the system operational. Production systems should set nproc, nofile, and as (address space) limits for all service accounts.

content_blocks.title: Key Resource Types Mnemonic
content_blocks.content:
**CROFMN** — the resource types you must know:
- **C**PU time (RLIMIT_CPU)
- **R**SS/memory (RLIMIT_RSS)
- **O**pen files (RLIMIT_NOFILE) — #1 cause of 'too many open files'
- **F**ile size (RLIMIT_FSIZE)
- **M**ax processes (RLIMIT_NPROC) — stops fork bombs
- **N**ice priority (RLIMIT_NICE)

The most security-critical: NOFILE and NPROC.

content_blocks.title: Check Your Understanding
content_blocks.content:
Consider a production server running nginx, PostgreSQL, and a Java application:
1. Which service account needs the highest nofile limit and why?
2. What happens if you set a hard limit lower than the current soft limit?
3. Why might a developer complain after you add limits.conf entries?

Think about the tradeoff between security and functionality.

content_blocks.title: Mindset: Limits as Defense in Depth
content_blocks.content: Resource limits aren't your primary defense — they're your last line before a runaway process hits the kernel. Configure them for every service account, test thoroughly, and monitor. The 5 minutes you spend setting nproc and nofile beats the 5 hours of downtime from a fork bomb.
